title: Place cells, grid cells, and cognitive maps
text:
CHAPTER 9. MEMORY
SECTION 9.3. PLACE CELLS, GRID CELLS, AND COGNITIVE MAPS

Rats in mazes and maps in heads

In the first half of the twentieth century, behaviorist psychology dominated the study of learning in America. Behaviorists such as John B. Watson and later B. F. Skinner argued that psychology should study only observable behavior, and that learning consists of forming associations between stimuli and responses. A rat learning a maze, in this view, learns a chain of responses: turn left at the first junction, right at the second, and so on.

Edward Tolman, a psychologist at the University of California, Berkeley, disagreed. In a 1948 paper titled "Cognitive maps in rats and men," he summarized experiments suggesting that rats learn something more like a map of their environment. For example, rats that had explored a maze without reward (and showed little evidence of learning) quickly performed well once food was introduced, indicating "latent learning" that had happened during exploration. In other experiments, when a familiar route was blocked, rats could choose novel shortcuts toward a goal, suggesting that they knew where the goal was in space, not merely a sequence of turns. Tolman proposed that the brain builds a "cognitive map" of the environment that can be used flexibly.

Tolman's idea was considered speculative because there was no known neural mechanism for such a map. That changed in 1971.

Place cells

In 1971, John O'Keefe and his student Jonathan Dostrovsky, at University College London, published a short paper in Brain Research reporting recordings from single neurons in the hippocampus of freely moving rats. They found that some neurons fired only when the rat was in a particular location in its environment. As the rat moved around, one cell would fire when it was in one corner, another in the middle, another near a wall. O'Keefe called these "place cells," and the location where a cell fires is called its "place field."

Each place cell represents a specific location, and a population of place cells collectively covers the whole environment, so that the pattern of active cells at any moment indicates where the animal is. In 1978, O'Keefe and Lynn Nadel published a book titled The Hippocampus as a Cognitive Map, arguing that the hippocampus is the neural substrate of Tolman's cognitive map.

Key properties of place cells, established over many years of research:

- Place fields are typically stable for a given environment over days or weeks.
- In a new environment, place fields form within minutes of exploration.
- Different environments are represented by different, apparently unrelated combinations of place fields; a cell that fires in one corner of one room may fire in the middle of another room or not at all. This switching of the representation between environments is called "remapping." It suggests that the hippocampus creates distinct, separated maps for different contexts, consistent with the pattern separation idea from section 9.1.
- Place cells use multiple sensory cues (visual landmarks, smells, textures) but can also maintain their firing in darkness, using self-motion information (path integration).
- Place cell firing is modulated by more than location: in some tasks, it depends on the direction of travel, the animal's goal, or the recent past and planned future path.

Spatial memory and the hippocampus

The connection between place cells and memory was supported by behavioral experiments. In 1981, Richard Morris introduced the "water maze" (now called the Morris water maze): a circular pool of opaque water with a small platform hidden just below the surface. Rats placed in the pool swim until they find the platform. Over trials, normal rats learn to swim directly to the platform from any starting point, using distant visual cues around the room. Rats with hippocampal lesions are severely impaired at this task, although they can learn to swim to a visible platform. In 1986, Morris and colleagues showed that blocking NMDA receptors in the hippocampus with the drug AP5 impaired learning in the water maze, linking NMDA-dependent plasticity (section 7.2) to spatial memory. In the 1990s, studies in genetically modified mice, including work in Susumu Tonegawa's laboratory with mice lacking NMDA receptors specifically in CA1 (reported in 1996 by Joe Tsien and colleagues), showed impaired spatial learning and less precise place fields, strengthening the link between synaptic plasticity, place cells, and memory.

Theta rhythm and phase precession

When a rat explores, the hippocampal local field potential (the summed electrical activity recorded by an electrode) shows a prominent oscillation at about 6 to 10 Hz, called the theta rhythm. In 1993, O'Keefe and Michael Recce discovered that place cells fire at systematically changing phases of the theta cycle as the rat moves through the place field: as the rat enters the field, the cell fires late in the theta cycle; as it moves through, it fires progressively earlier. This "phase precession" means that within each theta cycle, place cells whose fields the rat has recently passed through fire first, followed by cells for the current location, then cells for upcoming locations. Each theta cycle thus contains a compressed sequence representing the recent past, present, and near future. This temporal code carries information beyond firing rate alone, and the compressed sequences are well suited for Hebbian learning of sequences through STDP (section 7.2), since cells representing successive locations fire within milliseconds of each other.

Head direction cells

Place cells tell the animal where it is. Another class of neurons tells it which way it is facing. In 1984, James Ranck Jr. reported neurons in the rat's dorsal presubiculum (part of the hippocampal formation) that fired when the rat's head pointed in a particular direction in the horizontal plane, regardless of its location. Jeffrey Taube, Robert Muller, and Ranck characterized these "head direction cells" in detail in 1990. Each cell has a preferred direction, and the population covers all directions, like a neural compass. Head direction cells have since been found in several connected brain regions, including the anterodorsal thalamus and the entorhinal cortex.

A striking demonstration of a neural compass in an insect came in 2015, when Johannes Seelig and Vivek Jayaraman, imaging neurons in the central complex of the fruit fly brain, found a "bump" of activity that moved around a ring-shaped structure (the ellipsoid body) as the fly turned, tracking its heading, even in darkness. This is a physical realization of the "ring attractor" models that theorists had proposed for head direction systems, in which a localized bump of activity in a ring of recurrently connected neurons can be moved by angular velocity inputs.

Grid cells

The most surprising discovery came in 2005. May-Britt Moser and Edvard Moser, at the Norwegian University of Science and Technology in Trondheim (they had trained partly with John O'Keefe and with Richard Morris), recorded from the medial entorhinal cortex, the region that provides major input to the hippocampus. In a paper in Nature led by their student Torkel Hafting, they reported neurons that fired at multiple locations in the environment, and these locations formed a strikingly regular triangular (hexagonal) grid pattern that tiled the entire space. They called them "grid cells."

Properties of grid cells:

- Each grid cell fires at the vertices of a regular triangular lattice covering the environment.
- Nearby grid cells share the same grid spacing and orientation but have different spatial phases (their grids are shifted relative to each other), so together they cover all locations.
- Grid spacing increases in steps along the dorsal-to-ventral axis of the entorhinal cortex, from a few tens of centimeters to several meters in rats. Hanne Stensola, Tor Stensola, and colleagues showed in 2012 that grid cells are organized into discrete "modules," with the spacing ratio between successive modules roughly constant (on the order of 1.4 in their data).
- Grid patterns persist in darkness, indicating that they are generated largely by path integration of self-motion signals (speed and direction), with sensory landmarks used to correct accumulated errors.

Other spatial cell types were found in and near the entorhinal cortex, including "border cells" (firing along walls or edges of the environment, reported by Trygve Solstad, Charlotte Boccara, and colleagues in 2008), "speed cells" (firing rate proportional to running speed, Emilio Kropff and colleagues in 2015), and "object vector cells" (firing at particular distances and directions from objects). Related "boundary vector cells" had been predicted theoretically by Neil Burgess and colleagues and reported in the subiculum.

John O'Keefe, May-Britt Moser, and Edvard Moser shared the 2014 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine "for their discoveries of cells that constitute a positioning system in the brain."

How might grid cells work?

Grid cells are among the most mathematically elegant phenomena in neuroscience, and they have attracted many theoretical models. Two main classes:

Continuous attractor network models. In these models, grid cells are arranged in a network with a specific connectivity pattern: each cell excites cells with similar grid phases and inhibits others, so that the network settles into a stable pattern of activity "bumps" arranged on a hexagonal lattice in the neural sheet. Velocity inputs shift the activity pattern across the neural sheet in proportion to the animal's movement, so that the pattern tracks the animal's position by path integration. Yoram Burak and Ila Fiete showed in 2009 that such models can integrate velocity accurately over long distances. The hexagonal pattern arises naturally because a hexagonal arrangement of bumps is the most efficient packing in two dimensions given the lateral inhibition. A key prediction of these models is that the relationships between grid cells (their relative phases) should be preserved across environments and even during sleep, and this has been supported by experiments. In 2022, Richard Gardner, Erik Hermansen, Marius Pachitariu, and colleagues in the Moser lab, recording from hundreds of grid cells simultaneously with Neuropixels probes, reported that the joint activity of grid cells in a module lies on a toroidal (doughnut-shaped) manifold, exactly as predicted by continuous attractor models with periodic boundary conditions.

Oscillatory interference models. Earlier models proposed that grid patterns arise from interference between oscillations whose frequencies depend on running velocity in particular directions, related to theta rhythm. These models have faced difficulties, for example with grid cells found in bats, which lack continuous theta oscillations, though they remain part of the theoretical discussion.

Why a grid?

Why would the brain represent space with periodic grids at multiple scales? Theoretical work has shown that a set of grid modules with different spacings forms a highly efficient code for position. Ila Fiete, Yoram Burak, and Ted Brookings argued in 2008 that grid cells encode position in a way similar to a residue number system: each module encodes position modulo its own spacing (like the phase of a periodic signal), and combining several modules with different spacings specifies position uniquely over a very large range, with high resolution. Xue-Xin Wei, Jason Prentice, and Vijay Balasubramanian showed in 2015 that, under certain assumptions, an optimal ratio between successive module spacings should be close to the square root of e (about 1.65) or, in another formulation, around 1.4 to 1.7, roughly consistent with experimental data.

For an engineer, this is similar to how a vernier scale or a set of gears with different periods can measure a large quantity precisely, or how GPS combines signals, or how Fourier components at different frequencies can represent a function. The grid code can be seen as a kind of multi-scale periodic encoding of position.

Beyond physical space

An exciting development in the last decade is evidence that the hippocampal-entorhinal system represents not only physical space but also abstract "spaces." Some examples:

- Place-cell-like and grid-like codes for non-spatial variables. Dmitriy Aronov, Rhino Nevers, and David Tank reported in 2017 that rats manipulating a sound frequency with a joystick had hippocampal and entorhinal neurons that fired at specific frequencies, analogous to place fields in a "sound space."
- Grid-like signals in humans. Christian Doeller, Caswell Barry, and Neil Burgess reported in 2010 fMRI signals in human entorhinal cortex consistent with grid cells during virtual navigation, using a method that detects six-fold rotational symmetry in the signal as a function of movement direction. Alexandra Constantinescu, Jill O'Reilly, and Timothy Behrens reported in 2016 similar hexagonally symmetric signals when people navigated an abstract two-dimensional "space" of bird shapes varying in neck and leg length.
- Time cells. Howard Eichenbaum, Christopher MacDonald, and colleagues reported in 2011 hippocampal neurons that fired at specific moments during a delay period, as if marking time, analogous to place cells marking locations.

These findings support a general view, championed by Eichenbaum, Behrens, and others, that the hippocampal-entorhinal system provides a general mechanism for organizing knowledge in relational structures, a "cognitive map" in a broad sense, of which physical space is one example. Behrens and colleagues proposed in a 2018 Neuron review, "What is a cognitive map? Organizing knowledge for flexible behavior," that the same neural machinery could support inference in many domains.

Bridge to AI: grid cells in artificial networks

Grid cells have become a meeting point for neuroscience and AI.

In 2018, Andrea Banino, Caswell Barry, and colleagues at DeepMind published a paper in Nature, "Vector-based navigation using grid-like representations in artificial agents." They trained a recurrent neural network (an LSTM) to perform path integration: given velocity inputs, predict position (represented as activity in simulated place cells and head direction cells). Units with grid-like firing patterns emerged in the network's hidden layer, without being built in. When this network was incorporated into a reinforcement learning agent, the agent could navigate to goals using shortcuts, and its performance depended on the grid-like units. In the same year, Christopher Cueva and Xue-Xin Wei reported similar emergence of grid-like units in recurrent networks trained for path integration.

Subsequent work, including by Ben Sorscher, Gabriel Mel, Surya Ganguli, and Samuel Ocko (2019), clarified that grid-like units emerge only under certain conditions (such as particular choices of place cell tuning and non-negativity constraints), and Rylan Schaeffer, Mikail Khona, and Ila Fiete argued in 2022 that many reported "emergent" grid cells in artificial networks depended heavily on specific design choices, cautioning against overinterpreting such results. This debate is a good example of the care needed when claiming that a network "explains" a neural phenomenon.

James Whittington, Timothy Behrens, and colleagues proposed the Tolman-Eichenbaum Machine (TEM) in 2020, a network model that learns to separate the abstract structure of an environment (represented by grid-like codes, as in entorhinal cortex) from its specific sensory contents (combined in hippocampus-like conjunctive codes). TEM generalizes structural knowledge across environments and reproduces many properties of place and grid cells, including remapping. In 2022, Whittington, Joseph Warren, and Behrens reported that the transformer architecture, when given a particular kind of positional encoding and trained on similar tasks, is closely related to TEM, and that its representations resemble place and grid cells. This suggests a deep connection between hippocampal computation and the transformer models used in modern AI.

Finally, grid cells inspire engineering in robotics. RatSLAM, developed by Michael Milford, Gordon Wyeth, and colleagues in Australia in the 2000s, is a robot navigation system inspired by rodent place cells, head direction cells, and attractor networks, which has been used to map large outdoor environments with a camera. Simultaneous localization and mapping (SLAM) is a standard problem in mobile robotics, and the brain's solution, combining path integration with landmark correction in attractor networks, has been a source of ideas.

Summary

- Tolman (1948) proposed that rats learn cognitive maps rather than response chains.
- O'Keefe and Dostrovsky (1971) discovered hippocampal place cells that fire at specific locations; O'Keefe and Nadel (1978) proposed the hippocampus as a cognitive map.
- Place cells remap between environments, show theta phase precession, and depend on NMDA receptors for stability; hippocampal damage impairs spatial memory in the Morris water maze.
- Head direction cells act as a neural compass; a ring attractor was observed in the fruit fly.
- May-Britt and Edvard Moser discovered grid cells (2005), which fire on a hexagonal lattice and are organized into modules; O'Keefe and the Mosers shared the 2014 Nobel Prize.
- Continuous attractor models explain grid cells and predicted the toroidal population structure later observed.
- Grid codes are efficient multi-scale periodic codes; the hippocampal-entorhinal system may map abstract spaces as well.
- Grid-like units emerge in some trained recurrent networks; TEM and transformers are linked to hippocampal computation; RatSLAM brings these ideas to robotics.
